title: After the Rain

author.name: Adaeze Nwosu
author.bio: Adaeze Nwosu is a Lagos-born poet whose work explores memory, place, and the rhythms of everyday West African life. Her debut collection was shortlisted for the Wole Soyinka Prize.

description: A meditation on what remains after a storm passes — the quiet clarity of wet streets, the smell of earth, and the strange relief of things that have been washed away.
content:
The gutters carry
what the sky no longer needs —
old names, cold light.

I step outside
into the afterwards of rain,
the street still blinking
like something woken
from a dream it doesn't want to leave.

Everything is clean
the way a confession is clean —
not innocent, but lighter,
the weight redistributed
into puddles and drains.

A woman sweeps her threshold.
The broom makes the sound
of a sentence being revised,
stroke by stroke,
until it means something
more honest than before.

The mango tree shrugs
water from its shoulders.
Even the trees know
how to let things go.

I have been practicing.

A child runs past,
bare feet slapping the wet tar,
laughing at nothing,
laughing at everything —
at the sheer comedy
of being alive and wet
on a Thursday.

I want to be that.
I want to be that unserious
about joy.

The sky is still dark
at the edges,
but look:
right there, above the compound wall,
a thin blade of gold
where the sun
is trying again.

It always tries again.

That is the part
they never put in poems —
not the storm,
not the aftermath,
but the sun's stubborn,
unironic return.

Every time.
Without fail.
As if it has never heard
of giving up.

title: Inheritance

author.name: Marcus Webb
author.bio: Marcus Webb grew up in South London and writes about family, class, and the inherited silences of working-class British life. He is the author of two poetry pamphlets.

description: A son reads his father's hands like a map of unlived lives, tracing the calluses and scars of a man who gave everything except the words to say so.
content:
My father's hands were maps
of every road he didn't take —
I trace them still at night.

The callus at the base of his right thumb:
that's the factory, 1987 to 2003.
Sixteen years of the same lever,
the same resistance,
the same small victory of repetition.

He never spoke of it as sacrifice.
That is the thing about men like him —
they perform love in the key of silence,
in overtime and packed lunches,
in the annual holiday to the same caravan
because the children liked it the first time
and he had memorised their happiness.

I find his old work gloves
in the bottom of a box
and put my hands inside them.
They are too wide.
They will always be too wide.

This is the shape of what I am
trying to inherit:
not the gloves themselves
but the life that stretched them so.

He had a laugh
that started slow,
like a car on a cold morning,
then opened up
into something generous and unguarded.
I have been chasing that laugh
for fifteen years.

Sometimes I catch a glimpse of it
in my own mirror —
usually at the wrong moment,
at something that wouldn't be funny
to anyone else.

He taught me three things
without meaning to:
how to hold a door,
how to wait without fidgeting,
and how to love people
from just far enough away
that they never know the cost.

I am unlearning the last one.

It is slow work.

But then, so was the factory.
So was everything
that lasted.

title: Sea Glass

author.name: Priya Menon
author.bio: Priya Menon is a poet and translator from Mumbai. She writes primarily in English and Malayalam, and her work has appeared in Granta, The Kenyon Review, and numerous international anthologies.

description: Grief, like sea glass, is something the ocean takes and slowly, tenderly softens — returning it changed, smoothed of its sharpest edges, almost beautiful.
content:
The ocean softens
everything it swallows whole —
even grief, even you.

I found a piece of green glass
between two rocks at low tide,
its edges worn to nothing,
no trace of the bottle it had been,
no memory of the hand that dropped it,
or the deck it fell from,
or the year.

Just green.
Just smooth.
Just asking to be held.

I wonder sometimes
if the dead are like this —
not gone,
but processed.
Tumbled and rearranged
by currents we can't see
into something the living
can finally pick up
without bleeding.

You were sharp for so long.

For years after you left,
everything I touched
came back with your name on it.
The smell of cardamom.
A particular blue.
The sound of rain on a tin roof
at three in the morning
in a house that no longer exists.

Sharps. All of it. Sharps.

But the ocean works slowly,
thank god,
and has no deadline.

Now when I think of you
there is still weight to it,
still colour,
but the edges are gone.
I can run my thumb across the memory
and only feel the smoothness,
the warmth the glass holds
from the sun.

I put it in my coat pocket
and walked home.

The ocean kept working
behind me.
It always keeps working.
For all of us,
it keeps working.

title: Harmattan

author.name: Kofi Asante-Mensah
author.bio: Kofi Asante-Mensah is a Ghanaian poet and essayist whose work draws on Akan oral traditions and urban Accra. He lectures in African Literature at the University of Ghana.

description: The dry season wind that sweeps down from the Sahara carries not just dust but memory, longing, and a particular kind of homesickness that has no name in English.
content:
The harmattan arrives without announcement,
as all important things do —
not a storm but a presence,
a whitening of the air,
as if the world has decided
to rehearse its own forgetting.

The skin learns the language of dry.
The lips crack and speak it.
The eyes redden with argument.

My grandmother called it
the old breath of the north,
as if the desert itself
were sighing at us,
missing something
it had long ago put down.

We all have that breath in us.

The mango leaves turn
from green to a greenish-grey,
covered in fine dust
like old photographs
left too long in a drawer.
Everything from this season
looks like something
you are in the process of remembering.

At night the cold is a surprise —
it always is, every year,
as if we forget between seasons
that the desert does not keep the heat,
that it gives everything to the day
and takes it all back at sundown.

Generosity and cruelty
are sometimes the same gesture.

I have sat on this veranda
for thirty-seven harmattans.
I have watched the dust make the sun
into a copper coin
you could look at directly,
as if it had humbled itself for once,
dimmed itself to something human.

My father would stand here too
and say nothing.

I am learning the value of that —
of standing in the dry, particulate air
and saying nothing,
of letting the season
do the speaking,
of knowing that some years
the most honest thing you can offer
the world
is your quiet presence in it.

title: Night Train, Somewhere Between

author.name: Elena Vasquez
author.bio: Elena Vasquez is a Mexican-American poet raised on the US-Mexico border. Her work interrogates migration, belonging, and the geography of in-between places. She is a recipient of the National Book Award.

description: On an overnight train between two cities, between two languages, between two versions of herself, a woman takes stock of everything she is carrying.
content:
The window gives me back my face
laid over the dark country outside —
a double exposure,
everything I am
projected onto everything I'm passing through.

I have been on this train before.
Not this train. All trains.
Every train is the same train
if you are the kind of person
who leaves.

I carry two languages
like two coats.
One is always slightly wrong for the weather.

In Spanish I am softer.
I laugh more easily.
The words come out of me
like something I was born with,
which I was.

In English I am precise.
I can name things that don't exist
in the other language.
I can protect myself
with the clinical distance
of a borrowed vocabulary.

My mother called America
como el norte — as if it were
a direction rather than a place,
a gesture toward something
rather than the thing itself.

I have been gesturing north
my whole life.

The man across from me is asleep,
his mouth slightly open,
going somewhere in the way
only the unconscious can —
totally, without luggage,
without the performance of arrival.

I envy him.

I am always preparing
to explain myself.

At the border, years ago,
a guard asked me:
which side do you belong to?

I said: both.

He said: pick one.

I have been on this train since.

The lights of a town
flash past, then nothing,
then the lights of another town,
and I realize:
the in-between is also a place.

I live here.
I have always lived here.
In the window, in the dark between cities,
in the language between languages,
in the face that is both faces
and neither —

here, here, here.

title: What the Forest Kept

author.name: Sigrid Halvorsen
author.bio: Sigrid Halvorsen is a Norwegian poet and environmental writer whose collections have been translated into fourteen languages. She writes extensively about the Norwegian wilderness and ecological grief.

description: A slow walk through an ancient forest becomes a reckoning with what the natural world holds in trust for us — and what we have already lost without noticing.
content:
The oldest trees here
have been listening
since before anyone thought
to write anything down.

They have heard the wolves.
They remember the wolves.
In the rings of their silence
the wolves are still running.

I put my hand on the bark
of a birch that was already a hundred years old
when my grandmother was born,
and feel what language cannot hold:
the long grammar of patience,
the syntax of roots
that go down and down
until they find something
cold and certain and old
to hold onto.

The forest does not mourn
what it has lost.
Or if it does, it mourns
in a frequency I cannot hear —
some low note below language,
below grief,
in the register of simple continuance.

This is what I have come to learn.

How to keep going
without making the keeping-going
into a performance.

How to grow without announcement.

How to hold the dead —
all the dead birds and seasons
and centuries of fallen things —
inside you as nutrients,
as the very stuff
you are made of.

A deer steps between two trees
and disappears.

The forest closes behind her
like a sentence
that needs no ending.

I have been crying
and hadn't noticed.

That is something the trees can teach:
how to do the necessary things
without needing to know you're doing them.

The light here
is the colour of something
you loved as a child
and can no longer name.

I stay until the names stop mattering.
I stay until I am
just another thing
the forest is keeping.

title: My City at 3 AM

author.name: Jae-won Oh
author.bio: Jae-won Oh is a Seoul-based poet and urban photographer. His work is interested in the late-night ecology of modern cities — who moves through them after dark, and what they are looking for.

description: Seoul stripped of its daylight self — the neon still burning, the streets half-empty, a city between its public and its private face, caught in the vulnerability of almost-silence.
content:
At 3 AM the city
is finally honest.

The storefronts close their arguments.
The traffic stops performing urgency.
The neon signs keep burning
out of habit,
advertising to nobody,
still believing in the possibility
of a customer.

I find myself here often —
not insomnia exactly,
more like an appointment
I forgot to cancel
with the version of myself
that only comes out in the dark.

A delivery rider passes
on a silent electric bike,
headlights sweeping the wet street.
He is the 3 AM economy:
he is delivering urgency
to someone who cannot wait until morning
for ramen, for beer,
for the small comfort
of a hot thing arriving at your door
when everything else is closed.

I love him for this.

The Han River does not sleep.
It just keeps its own hours,
passing through the city
like a thought
that has been here longer
than the city has,
that will still be moving
long after the city
stops.

Below the bridge,
a fisherman
too patient to be practical.
His line in the water.
His thermos. His stillness.

There is an argument
that the people who are awake
at 3 AM
are the realest people —
not performing their lives
for anyone,
just existing,
just moving through
the stripped-back city
on their own private business.

I am one of them.

I buy a coffee from a machine
that has been awake
for longer than I have.

It is terrible.
I drink it slowly
and watch the city
take practice breaths
before the morning starts again.

title: A Letter to the Body I Was Ashamed Of

author.name: Amara Osei
author.bio: Amara Osei is a British-Ghanaian poet and spoken word artist. Her debut collection, 'Tender Architecture', was a Sunday Times Book of the Year. She writes about Blackness, womanhood, and embodiment.

description: A direct, tender address to the body — its history of being judged, hidden, and apologised for, and the long work of returning to it as a home.
content:
I owe you an apology
for all the years I spoke of you
in the third person,
as if you were a problem
someone else had given me
to solve.

I am sorry for the mirrors
I stood in front of
and negotiated with.
As if you were a price.
As if you could be haggled down
to something more acceptable
if I just held the right posture,
ate the right things,
wore the right colour.

You were never the problem.

I handed you to other people
and watched them judge you
and took their verdicts home
and posted them on the inside of my ribs
where I could find them easily,
where I could refer to them
when I needed to feel small.

That was not wisdom.
That was just damage,
passing itself off as self-knowledge.

Here is what I know now:

You have carried me
through every difficult morning.
You have woken up
when you had every reason not to.
You have held my grief
in the chest and the throat
and the stomach
and let me feel it
rather than storing it
until it turned to stone.

You are made of the same material
as the things I find beautiful —
the same carbon,
the same ancient stuff,
the same unremarkable miracle
of matter deciding to be alive
for a while.

The stretch marks on your hips:
a map of the years.
I have started to love them
the way I love old handwriting —
for the evidence of time
in something I thought I owned.

You are not mine to own.
You are mine to live in.

I am home now.
I am trying to be home now.
Thank you for waiting.

title: The Beekeeper's Daughter

author.name: Ruth Adeyemi
author.bio: Ruth Adeyemi is a Nigerian-British poet whose work weaves together Yoruba mythology and contemporary British life. She was the first Black woman to win the Forward Prize for Best First Collection.

description: A daughter remembers her father's bees and what they taught her: about patience, about the acceptance of small stings, about the strange sweetness that requires community to exist.
content:
My father kept his bees
at the bottom of the garden,
past the pawpaw tree,
past the standpipe,
in the corner where the garden
became something wilder
and less negotiated.

He visited them the way
he visited church —
religiously, quietly,
with the particular peace
of a man who has found
the thing that asks nothing of him
except his attention.

I was afraid of them.
This seemed to him
not a failing
but a starting point.

"Adunola," he would say,
using my full name
the way he only did
when he meant something —
"the bees are not interested in your fear.
They are only interested in the flower.
Be the flower."

I was eight.
I did not know how to be a flower.
I still sometimes don't.

But I learned to be still.
That was his first lesson:
stillness is not the absence of feeling.
It is feeling
without making the feeling
everyone else's emergency.

He showed me how to move
among them —
slowly, no perfume,
no sudden gestures,
no performance of confidence,
just the genuine article,
which the bees, he said,
could smell.

They could smell fear.
They could smell also:
fake calm.
The real thing only.

He was stung many times
and never once cursed.
He would look at the sting,
pull it out gently,
rub the spot,
and say:
"It's only paying attention."

I think of that
when the world stings me now —
when the meeting goes wrong,
when the phone call brings
what phone calls sometimes bring,
when I am misunderstood
in a language I have worked so hard
to be fluent in.

Only paying attention.

Something noticing
that I was close
to something it loves.

title: New Year, Same Stars

author.name: Lena Marchetti
author.bio: Lena Marchetti is an Italian poet living in Rome. Her work explores cyclical time, ritual, and the way human beings use celebration to briefly outrun their own mortality.

description: On the first night of a new year, the fireworks are done and the champagne is flat, and the only honest thing left is the sky — unchanged, indifferent, and somehow the most comforting thing there is.
content:
By midnight the promises
have already started to soften
at the edges,
becoming intentions,
then hopes,
then the vague shape of hopes,
then just the feeling
that something should be different now.

This is fine.
This is human.
This is the whole point.

We do not celebrate the new year
because we believe in it.
We celebrate it
because we need the ritual
of pretending time has a door.

Come in, we say.
Sit down.
Be kinder than the last one.

After the fireworks,
after the kissing,
after the messages sent
to people we only remember
when the calendar turns,
I go outside
and look up.

The stars are exactly
where I left them.

Orion is not interested
in the Gregorian calendar.
Cassiopeia has not adjusted
for the new year.
The Plough is still pointing
where it has always pointed —
north, fixed, patient,
outlasting every civilisation
that has ever needed it
to navigate.

This is the thing
nobody puts on a card:

that the most comforting thing in the sky
is its complete indifference.

The stars do not celebrate.
The stars do not grieve.
The stars are not keeping score
of what you did wrong
and what you promised.

They are simply there,
watching your little fireworks
with the patience
of things that have watched
a billion years of little fireworks
and know:

it is enough.
It is enough to be here.
It is enough to have tried.
It is enough to look up
and know you are looking
at the same lights
everyone has ever looked at
when they needed
to feel small enough
to start again.
